scope: Direct primary-work chapter/section review of Augustine and Eusebius, cross-referenced against existing Oxford/Newman Catena source segments; not a complete mining census
sourceAnchorPolicy: Source-language short anchors for verification, not complete author answers. Editorial natural questions are never attributed as verbatim Father speech.
englishTranslationPolicy: No new independently publishable English translation created; existing Catena quotes remain owned by canonical corpus. External Greek translation rights and accuracy are not cleared.
verification: Primary online Greek/Latin text and specified canonical Catena fragment were manually inspected; independent critical edition, second-reader, doctrinal and licensing approvals remain outstanding.

records.author: Augustine of Hippo
records.sourceAnchor: Quod Zacharias orans pro populo audit ab angelo
records.readerFacingQuestionEditorial: Why was Zacharias told that his prayer was heard?

catenaMatches.sourceTextAnchor: Now here we must first consider

observations: Latin work II.1; Catena excerpt's parenthetical citation reads 'l. i. q. l.' and conflicts with consulted Latin placement; preserve conflict pending independent editorial verification.
The Latin source treats his prayer on behalf of the people, not necessarily an explicit literal question spoken by Augustine.

records.author: Augustine of Hippo
records.readerFacingQuestionEditorial: Why did Jesus command the healed leper to offer the Mosaic sacrifice?

catenaMatches.sourceTextAnchor: He seems here to approve of the sacrifice

observations: Latin II.3 gives a reason by distinguishing typological Mosaic sacrifices from Christ's sacrifice.
Do not treat the modern reader question as Augustine's verbatim Latin wording.

records.author: Augustine of Hippo
records.sourceAnchor: quomodo potuerit duos patres habere Ioseph
records.readerFacingQuestionEditorial: How could Joseph have two fathers in Matthew and Luke?

catenaMatches.sourceTextAnchor: He is more properly called his son

observations: In II.5 Augustine discusses alternatives; his Latin later calls the levirate alternative weaker (illa videtur infirma quam secundo loco posuimus).
The Catena passage from De Consensu Evangelistarum in Matthew 1:16 is a distinct Augustine work, not a duplicate excerpt from Quaestiones.
Do not convert alternatives into a single claim that Augustine conclusively settled the historical genealogy.

records.author: Augustine of Hippo
records.sourceAnchor: Quid sibi velit quod septuaginta septem personae
records.readerFacingQuestionEditorial: What does the number seventy-seven mean in Luke's genealogy?

catenaMatches.sourceTextAnchor: But most fitly with regard to our baptized Lord

observations: The Latin starts the numbered question II.6 with an explicit inquiry; Catena explicitly cites Quæst. Ev. lib. ii. qu. 6.
This is Augustine's theological reading of the number, not an arithmetical proof that all count variants use the same method.

records.author: Augustine of Hippo
records.sourceAnchor: Sicut enim fuit Ionas in ventre ceti
records.readerFacingQuestionEditorial: How can the three days and three nights of the burial be understood?

catenaMatches.sourceTextAnchor: Some, not knowing the Scripture manner

observations: Latin I.7 supplies a part-for-whole temporal reckoning for Matthew 12:40.
The linked Catena Augustine selection is from De Consensu Evangelistarum, so it must not be labelled a direct Quaestiones excerpt.
The Catena source ordinal of the related excerpt is checked by the validation script, not a claim of identical source work.

records.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
records.sourceAnchor: Τί δὴ οὖν εἰς τὸ προταθὲν τοῦτο πρόβλημα
records.readerFacingQuestionEditorial: Why do Matthew and Luke trace Joseph through different ancestors?

catenaMatches.sourceTextAnchor: Let us then more carefully explain

observations: The Greek supplement presents the genealogy difference as an articulated problem, and contains Eusebius's response; the modern English translation on the host has not been cleared for reuse.
Catena's Eusebius extract on Luke 3:23 is a strong thematic/textual parallel; direct edition-level identity is not certified.

The Catena's Eusebius Hist. Eccles. I.7 genealogical narrative often transmits Julius Africanus. Preserve embedded author/voice; do not call Africanus's quoted solution Eusebius's independently authored answer.

records.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
records.sourceAnchor: Ἠρώτας δὲ τὸ πρῶτον· Αʹ. Πῶς παρὰ μὲν τῷ Ματθαίῳ
records.readerFacingQuestionEditorial: How can the resurrection timing in Matthew and Mark be reconciled?
observations: The question is introduced as Marinus's, not as an original interrogative posed by Eusebius himself.
Eusebius discusses more than one solution, including a hypothetical textual exclusion and an alternative punctuation reading; one solution alone must not be presented as his unqualified judgement.
No directly matched Catena Eusebius excerpt was identified for these two Gospel pericopes; the external text should be indexed as a separate source, not backfilled into an existing Father bubble.
The Greek/English text displayed by Catholic Library may involve modern edition/translation rights; no wholesale copying or automated publication.
